title: Greetings
grammarNote: Use 'buenos' for masculine/neutral greetings, 'buenas' for feminine. Time of day matters: buenos días (morning), buenas tardes (afternoon), buenas noches (evening/night).

phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Buenos días' literally means 'good days' — used as a morning greeting until roughly noon.
phrases.grammarNote: 'Buenos' agrees with the plural masculine noun 'días'; never say 'buena día'.
phrases.memoryHook: Think of it as 'way' plus 'nos', meaning 'us' — 'our good day begins'.

practiceItems.prompt: ¿Qué dices a las 8 de la mañana?

phrases.vocabularyIntro: '¿Cómo estás?' is the standard informal way to ask how someone is doing; use it with friends, family, and peers.
phrases.grammarNote: 'Estás' is the informal tú form of estar; the formal usted equivalent is '¿Cómo está?' — the tú form always ends in -ás.
phrases.memoryHook: Cómo estás is your casual check-in — the everyday way to ask 'how's it going?'

practiceItems.prompt: Quieres preguntarle a un amigo cómo se siente. ¿Qué le preguntas?

phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Estoy bien' is the standard reply to '¿Cómo estás?', using estar for a temporary state or feeling rather than a permanent trait.
phrases.grammarNote: 'Estoy' comes from estar (temporary states/feelings), not ser (permanent traits) — use estar whenever you're describing how you feel right now.
phrases.memoryHook: Estoy bien pairs 'I am' with 'well' — the simplest possible status update.

practiceItems.prompt: Un amigo te pregunta cómo estás y te sientes bien. ¿Qué le respondes?

phrases.native: Nice to meet you / Pleased to meet you
phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Mucho gusto' literally means 'much pleasure' — the standard fixed phrase said right after meeting someone for the first time.

exampleSentence.native: Nice to meet you, I'm Ana.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Mucho gusto' is a fixed exclamation and doesn't conjugate — it stays exactly the same regardless of who's speaking or being addressed.
phrases.memoryHook: Mucho gusto = 'much pleasure' — imagine a warm handshake the moment you say it.

practiceItems.prompt: Acabas de conocer a alguien nuevo. ¿Qué le dices?

phrases.vocabularyIntro: '¿Cuál es tu nombre?' is the direct, informal way to ask someone's name; 'tu' (your, informal) matches the tú register used throughout this lesson.
phrases.grammarNote: 'Cuál' (which/what) is used here rather than 'qué' because you're selecting from a set of possible names, not asking for a definition.
phrases.memoryHook: Cuál es tu nombre — picture pointing at a name tag and asking 'which one is yours?'

practiceItems.prompt: Quieres saber el nombre de alguien que acabas de conocer. ¿Qué le preguntas?

phrases.vocabularyIntro: 'Me llamo...' (literally 'I call myself...') is the standard reflexive way to state your name, more common in everyday speech than 'Mi nombre es...'

exampleSentence.native: My name is Juan, nice to meet you.

phrases.grammarNote: 'Llamarse' is reflexive: me llamo, te llamas, se llama — the pronoun 'me' shows the calling happens to yourself.
phrases.memoryHook: Me llamo = 'I call myself' — you're literally introducing yourself by name.

practiceItems.prompt: Alguien te pregunta tu nombre y te llamas Juan. ¿Qué respondes?

dialogue.scenario: You run into a coworker in the morning at the office.

turns.speaker: npc
turns.native: Nice to meet you. What is your name?
